I'm starting this subverse off with one of my favorite pictures; an AIDS fighting fluorescent kitty!
I have questions. Why is it fluorescent? Does that help it somehow fight AIDS? Is it fighting AIDS because it HAS AIDS or is it like some sort of kitty-superhero?

It is fluorescent because they inserted a gene from a jellyfish that makes the cats cells produce green fluorescent proteins. The cool thing about making animals fluoresce like this is that you can tie the fluorescence to other proteins/things. In this case they made it so for every fluorescent protein expressed there would also be a potential AIDS fighting protein. Then they can take the cats that fluoresce and test different proteins to see how well they fight off AIDS.
So what you're saying is that we could attach the fluorescent protein to endorphins so that when people are really happy they will literally be beaming??
I don't know if I have ever heard of someone attaching fluorescent proteins to endorphins but that is the general idea. They have attached fluorescent proteins to calcium to watch a fish think.
Here is a source if you want to learn more about how transgenic cats help fight AIDS.

A little back story. My wife does most of the gardening. I'll help her out, but I follow her instructions and I don't know anything myself. She's away visiting family, and I've tried googling my problem but nothing comes up.

So basically, I have a mint, a chocolate mint, and a rosemary plant in my front yard. Recently, they've been getting this slimy white substance, almost like mucus or saliva, on their stems, between the leaves. It's been spreading pretty rapidly. What is it, and how do I get rid of it? I tried applying a fungicide but it didn't get rid of the stuff.

I thought it might be powdery mildew, but when I looked that up, it seemed to only grow on leaves and fruits, not stems, and it was always powdery. This stuff gets powdery if it dries, but it starts off snotty, and it grows primarily on the stems, not the leaves.

Picture: https://slimgur.com/image/fyy

It doesn't look like a bug. It looks like snot. I looked up spitbug spit, and it's all bubbly. This has no bubbles in it.

I would prune the heavily infected leaves (mint is so prolific anyway, you probably won't miss it!) and then wash the leaves with a diluted dish soap solution. Or rubbing alcohol.
